claim: Lower vertebrates contain adult stem cells (aSCs) that maintain homeostasis and drive un-exhaustive organismal growth.
source: While lower vertebrates contain adult stem cells (aSCs) that maintain homeostasis and drive un-exhaustive organismal growth, mammalian aSCs display mainly the homeostatic function.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a contrast to mammalian aSCs, establishing the context for the study.

claim: Mammalian aSCs display mainly the homeostatic function.
source: While lower vertebrates contain adult stem cells (aSCs) that maintain homeostasis and drive un-exhaustive organismal growth, mammalian aSCs display mainly the homeostatic function.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as established knowledge about mammalian stem cells.

claim: The medaka fish gill contains separate stem cell populations for homeostasis and growth.
source: Here, we use lineage analysis in the medaka fish gill to address aSCs and report separate stem cell populations for homeostasis and growth.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract, supported by lineage analysis experiments described throughout the manuscript.

claim: Gill stem cells are fate-restricted during the entire post-embryonic life.
source: These aSCs are fate-restricted during the entire post-embryonic life and even during re-generation paradigms.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data showing consistent recombination patterns throughout the manuscript.

claim: Gill stem cells are fate-restricted even during re-generation paradigms.
source: These aSCs are fate-restricted during the entire post-embryonic life and even during re-generation paradigms.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by ablation experiments shown in Figure 8.

claim: p53 mediates growth coordination among fate-restricted aSCs in the gill.
source: We use chimeric animals to demonstrate that p53 mediates growth coordination among fate-restricted aSCs, suggesting a hierarchical organisation among lineages in composite organs like the fish gill.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by chimera experiments shown in Figure 6.

claim: There is a hierarchical organisation among lineages in composite organs like the fish gill.
source: We use chimeric animals to demonstrate that p53 mediates growth coordination among fate-restricted aSCs, suggesting a hierarchical organisation among lineages in composite organs like the fish gill.
evidence: This is inferred from the p53 chimera experiments showing differential effects of mutations in different lineages.

claim: Homeostatic and growth aSCs are clonal.
source: Homeostatic and growth aSCs are clonal but differ in their topology
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by lineage tracing experiments showing that growth and homeostatic stem cells within a lineage share the same label.

claim: Homeostatic and growth aSCs differ in their topology.
source: Homeostatic and growth aSCs are clonal but differ in their topology
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated by the different locations of these stem cells along the filament as shown in multiple figures.

claim: Modifications in tissue architecture can convert the homeostatic zone into a growth zone.
source: modifications in tissue architecture can convert the homeostatic zone into a growth zone, indicating a leading role for the physical niche defining stem cell output.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by ablation experiments in Figure 8 showing that homeostatic domains can regenerate growth domains.

claim: Physical niches play a leading role in defining stem cell output.
source: modifications in tissue architecture can convert the homeostatic zone into a growth zone, indicating a leading role for the physical niche defining stem cell output.
evidence: This is inferred from the ablation experiments and stated as an interpretation in the abstract.

claim: Physical niches are main players to restrict aSCs to a homeostatic function in animals with fixed adult size.
source: We hypothesise that physical niches are main players to restrict aSCs to a homeostatic function in animals with fixed adult size.
evidence: This is presented as a hypothesis in the abstract based on the experimental findings.

claim: Higher vertebrates acquire a definitive body size around the time of their sexual maturation.
source: Higher vertebrates acquire a definitive body size around the time of their sexual maturation.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Mammalian adult stem cells mainly replace cells that are lost on a daily basis after sexual maturation.
source: Although many adult stem cells (aSCs) remain active and keep producing new cells afterwards, they mainly replace cells that are lost on a daily basis.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about mammalian stem cells in the introduction.

claim: Lower vertebrates like fish keep increasing their size even during adulthood.
source: On the other hand, lower vertebrates like fish keep increasing their size even during adulthood due to the capacity of aSCs to drive growth in parallel to maintaining organ homeostasis.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Lower vertebrates' aSCs can drive growth in parallel to maintaining organ homeostasis.
source: On the other hand, lower vertebrates like fish keep increasing their size even during adulthood due to the capacity of aSCs to drive growth in parallel to maintaining organ homeostasis.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: The basis for the different outputs between aSCs in lower and higher vertebrates is still not fully understood.
source: The basis for the different outputs between aSCs in lower and higher vertebrates is still not fully understood.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction to establish the knowledge gap.

claim: In pathological conditions mammalian aSCs exhibit the ability to drive growth.
source: It has been reported, however, that in pathological conditions mammalian aSCs exhibit the ability to drive growth, as best represented by cancer stem cells (CSCs) (Batlle and Clevers, 2017; Nassar and Blanpain, 2016; Clevers, 2011; Suvà et al., 2014; Quintana et al., 2008; Barker et al., 2009; Schepers et al., 2012; Boumahdi et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by multiple citations.

claim: Cancer stem cells represent mammalian aSCs that drive growth in pathological conditions.
source: It has been reported, however, that in pathological conditions mammalian aSCs exhibit the ability to drive growth, as best represented by cancer stem cells (CSCs) (Batlle and Clevers, 2017; Nassar and Blanpain, 2016; Clevers, 2011; Suvà et al., 2014; Quintana et al., 2008; Barker et al., 2009; Schepers et al., 2012; Boumahdi et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by multiple citations.

claim: The medaka gill works as a respiratory, sensory and osmoregulatory organ in most teleost fish.
source: We decided to address this question using the medaka gill, which works as a respiratory, sensory and osmoregulatory organ in most teleost fish.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge about gill function.

claim: Gills are permanently exposed to circulating water and therefore have a high turnover rate.
source: Gills are permanently exposed to circulating water and therefore have a high turnover rate (Chrétien and Pisam, 1986).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: Gill growth pace must guarantee oxygen supply to meet the energetic demands of growing organismal size.
source: Additionally, their growth pace must guarantee oxygen supply to meet the energetic demands of growing organismal size.
evidence: This is stated as a logical inference about gill function in the introduction.

claim: Gills are organised in four pairs of branchial arches.
source: Moving from the highest-level structure to the smallest, gills are organised in four pairs of branchial arches, a number which remains constant through the fish's life.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as an anatomical fact.

claim: The number of branchial arches remains constant through the fish's life.
source: Moving from the highest-level structure to the smallest, gills are organised in four pairs of branchial arches, a number which remains constant through the fish's life.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as an anatomical fact.

claim: Each branchial arch consists of two rows of an ever-increasing number of filaments that are added life-long at both extremes.
source: Each brachial arch consists of two rows of an ever-increasing number of filaments that are added life-long at both extremes (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Primary filaments have a core from which secondary filaments, or lamellae, protrude.
source: Primary filaments have a core from which secondary filaments, or lamellae, protrude.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as an anatomical description.

claim: The lamellae are the respiratory units of the organ.
source: The lamellae are the respiratory units of the organ, and new lamellae are continually produced within each filament (Wilson and Laurent, 2002).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: New lamellae are continually produced within each filament.
source: The lamellae are the respiratory units of the organ, and new lamellae are continually produced within each filament (Wilson and Laurent, 2002).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: Bigger fish display more filaments that are longer than those of smaller fish.
source: Bigger fish, therefore, display more filaments that are longer than those of smaller fish, and there is a direct correlation of filament length and number and the body size of the fish (Wilson and Laurent, 2002).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: There is a direct correlation of filament length and number and the body size of the fish.
source: Bigger fish, therefore, display more filaments that are longer than those of smaller fish, and there is a direct correlation of filament length and number and the body size of the fish (Wilson and Laurent, 2002).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: The gill contains oxygen-sensing cells similar to those found in the mammalian carotid body.
source: It contains oxygen-sensing cells (Jonz et al., 2004), similar to those found in the mammalian carotid body although with a different lineage history (Hockman et al., 2017)
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: Gill oxygen-sensing cells have a different lineage history than mammalian carotid body cells.
source: It contains oxygen-sensing cells (Jonz et al., 2004), similar to those found in the mammalian carotid body although with a different lineage history (Hockman et al., 2017)
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: The gill contains mitochondrial rich cells (MRCs) that regulate ion uptake and excretion.
source: and mitochondrial rich cells (MRCs) (Wilson and Laurent, 2002) that regulate ion uptake and excretion and are identified by a distinctive Na+, K+, ATPase activity.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: MRCs are identified by a distinctive Na+, K+, ATPase activity.
source: and mitochondrial rich cells (MRCs) (Wilson and Laurent, 2002) that regulate ion uptake and excretion and are identified by a distinctive Na+, K+, ATPase activity.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: Gill cell types include pavement cells, pillar cells, globe cells, chondrocytes and vascular cells.
source: Other cell types include pavement cells (respiratory cells of the gills), pillar cells (structural support for lamellae), globe cells (mucous secretory cells), chondrocytes (skeleton of the filaments) and vascular cells.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge about gill cell types.

claim: All gill cell types must be permanently produced in a coordinated manner during the post-embryonic life of fish.
source: All these cell types must be permanently produced in a coordinated manner during the post-embryonic life of fish.
evidence: This is stated as a logical inference in the introduction.

claim: Bona fide stem cells can only be identified and characterised by following their offspring for long periods to prove self-renewal.
source: Bona fide stem cells can only be identified and characterised by following their offspring for long periods to prove self-renewal, the defining feature of stem cells (Clevers and Watt, 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: Organ size increases during post-embryonic growth in medaka gills.
source: Enucleated entire gills of medaka at different post-embryonic times show that organ size increases during post-embryonic growth (left).
evidence: This is stated in Figure 1 legend and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The number of filaments per branchial arch is higher in bigger fish.
source: The number of filaments per branchial arch is higher in bigger fish - x axis represents fish length, and y axis the number of filaments in the second right branchial arch.
evidence: This is stated in Figure 1 legend and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: IdU incorporation in the adult gill reflects proliferating cells all along the longitudinal axis of a filament.
source: IdU incorporation in the adult gill reflects proliferating cells all along the longitudinal axis of a filament.
evidence: This is stated in Figure 1 legend and shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Branchial arches in medaka continue to expand along two axes well after sexual maturation.
source: Branchial arches in medaka continue to expand along these two axes well after sexual maturation (Figure 1B,C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 1B,C.

claim: When adult medaka fish are incubated with IdU for 48 hr, their gill filaments display a strong signal from the base to the top.
source: When adult medaka fish are incubated with IdU for 48 hr, their gill filaments display a strong signal from the base to the top (Figure 1D), which indicates the presence of mitotically active cells all along the filament's longitudinal axis.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The length of filaments increases from peripheral to central positions.
source: The length of filaments increases from peripheral to central positions (Figures 1A and 2A), regardless of the total number of filaments per branchial arch (Leguen, 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figures 1A and 2A, with additional citation support.

claim: The oldest and therefore longest filaments, of embryonic origin, locate to the centre of a branchial arch.
source: This particular arrangement suggests that the oldest and therefore longest filaments, of embryonic origin, locate to the centre of a branchial arch, while the new filaments are incorporated at the peripheral extremes either by stem cells (permanent) or progenitors (exhaustive).
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the observed arrangement in the Results section.

claim: New filaments are incorporated at the peripheral extremes of branchial arches.
source: This particular arrangement suggests that the oldest and therefore longest filaments, of embryonic origin, locate to the centre of a branchial arch, while the new filaments are incorporated at the peripheral extremes either by stem cells (permanent) or progenitors (exhaustive).
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the observed arrangement in the Results section.

claim: Post-embryonic filaments at the extreme of branchial arches were grouped in either labelled or non-labelled stretches.
source: When we analysed adult GaudíUbiq.iCRE GaudíRSG transgenic fish that had been induced for sparse recombination at old embryonic stages (nine dpf.), we observed that post-embryonic filaments at the extreme of branchial arches were grouped in either labelled or non-labelled stretches (Figure 2B,C, asterisks for labelled stretches and arrowheads for embryonic filaments) suggesting that they were generated by bona-fide stem cells.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2B,C.

claim: The grouping of labelled filaments suggests they were generated by bona-fide stem cells.
source: When we analysed adult GaudíUbiq.iCRE GaudíRSG transgenic fish that had been induced for sparse recombination at old embryonic stages (nine dpf.), we observed that post-embryonic filaments at the extreme of branchial arches were grouped in either labelled or non-labelled stretches (Figure 2B,C, asterisks for labelled stretches and arrowheads for embryonic filaments) suggesting that they were generated by bona-fide stem cells.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the experimental data in the Results section.

claim: For every gill analysed, the stem cell model explained the experimental data better than the progenitor cell model.
source: For every gill analysed, the stem cell model explained the experimental data better than the progenitor cell model (Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by computational modeling data.

claim: There exist growth stem cells at the peripheral extremes of branchial arches, which generate new filaments during the post-embryonic life in medaka.
source: Altogether, our data revealed the existence of growth stem cells at the peripheral extremes of branchial arches, which generate new filaments during the post-embryonic life in medaka.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the experimental and modeling data in the Results section.

claim: Previous data on stationary samples suggest that filaments grow from their tip.
source: Previous data on stationary samples suggest that filaments grow from their tip (Morgan, 1974)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by a citation.

claim: All filaments analysed contained a region deprived of IdU at the most distal tip.
source: Indeed, all filaments analysed contained a region deprived of IdU at the most distal tip (Figure 3B), what stays in agreement with the previous assumptions.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Clones at the proximal and middle part of the filament were small and restricted to one lamella.
source: We observed that clones at the proximal and middle part of the filament were small and restricted to one lamella, while the clones at the distal part contained hundreds of cells suggesting that they were generated by growth stem cells (Figure 3C,D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3C,D.

claim: Clones at the distal part of filaments contained hundreds of cells suggesting that they were generated by growth stem cells.
source: We observed that clones at the proximal and middle part of the filament were small and restricted to one lamella, while the clones at the distal part contained hundreds of cells suggesting that they were generated by growth stem cells (Figure 3C,D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3C,D.

claim: The apical part of each filament and the more peripheral filaments are devoid of IdU signal revealing the stereotypic growth of branchial arches.
source: The apical part of each filament and the more peripheral filaments are devoted of signal revealing the stereotypic growth of branchial arches.
evidence: This is stated in Figure 3 legend and shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Individual filaments had grown at comparable rates during the chase phase.
source: Interestingly, while we observed that the central filaments showed a longer basal signal that becomes shorter in more peripheral filaments, the upper non-labelled fraction seemed rather stable along the central-to-periphery axis of the branchial arch (Figure 3F). This suggested that individual filaments had grown at comparable rates during the chase phase, highlighting the coordinated activity of the stem cells that sustained length growth in each filament.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the IdU chase data in the Results section.

claim: The coordinated activity of stem cells sustains length growth in each filament.
source: This suggested that individual filaments had grown at comparable rates during the chase phase, highlighting the coordinated activity of the stem cells that sustained length growth in each filament.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the IdU chase data in the Results section.

claim: RNA-seq revealed differentiated cells in the middle region of filaments and undifferentiated cells at the apical domain.
source: RNA-seq revealed differentiated cells in the middle region of filaments and undifferentiated cells at the apical domain.
evidence: This is stated in Figure 3 legend and supported by RNA-seq data.

claim: Upregulated genes in the central domain included numerous membrane transporters and channels that are characteristic of the fish gill.
source: As expected, upregulated genes in the central domain included numerous membrane transporters and channels that are characteristic of the fish gill, typically present in ionocytes and MRC cells.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on RNA-seq analysis.

claim: GO analysis of RNA-seq data recognised the genes enriched in the central sample as 'Gill Tissue'.
source: Indeed, GO analysis of RNA-seq data using the DAVID bioinformatic resource (https://david.ncifcrf.gov/) recognised the genes enriched in the central sample as 'Gill Tissue' (UP_TISSUE: Gill).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on GO analysis of RNA-seq data.

claim: The major ontology class assigned to differential genes in the apical domain of filaments was 'Embryo'.
source: When analysing the differential genes in the apical domain of filaments, however, the major ontology class assigned was 'Embryo' (UP_TISSUE: Embryo), which is compatible with a region enriched in undifferentiated cells like stem cells and amplifying progenitors.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on GO analysis of RNA-seq data.

claim: The 'Embryo' ontology class is compatible with a region enriched in undifferentiated cells like stem cells and amplifying progenitors.
source: When analysing the differential genes in the apical domain of filaments, however, the major ontology class assigned was 'Embryo' (UP_TISSUE: Embryo), which is compatible with a region enriched in undifferentiated cells like stem cells and amplifying progenitors.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the GO analysis in the Results section.

claim: Neuroendocrine cells (NECs) are derived from the endoderm.
source: Previous experiments in zebrafish on labelling cell populations at early embryonic stages revealed that neuroendocrine cells (NECs) are derived from the endoderm (Hockman et al., 2017)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by a citation.

claim: Pillar cells have a neural crest origin.
source: while pillar cells have a neural crest origin (Mongera et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by a citation.

claim: Four different recombination patterns were identified illustrating the lineage of different types of growth stem cells.
source: Our analysis revealed the presence of four different recombination patterns illustrating the lineage of different types of growth stem cells (Figure 4C–F, patterns 1 to 4).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4C-F.

claim: Growth stem cells at the tip of gill filaments are fate-restricted.
source: Moreover, this lineage analysis approach showed that growth stem cells at the tip of gill filaments are indeed fate-restricted, and hence, the most apical domain of a filament hosts different growth stem cells with complementary potential.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the lineage analysis in the Results section.

claim: The most apical domain of a filament hosts different growth stem cells with complementary potential.
source: Moreover, this lineage analysis approach showed that growth stem cells at the tip of gill filaments are indeed fate-restricted, and hence, the most apical domain of a filament hosts different growth stem cells with complementary potential.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the lineage analysis in the Results section.

claim: Recombined filaments displayed the same lineage patterns spanning from their base to their tip.
source: Noticeable, recombined filaments displayed the same lineage patterns spanning from their base, that is juvenile domain, to their tip, that is adult domain, (Figure 4C–F) (N > 200 recombined filaments) indicating that growth stem cells maintain both their activity and their potency during a lifetime.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4C-F.

claim: Growth stem cells maintain both their activity and their potency during a lifetime.
source: Noticeable, recombined filaments displayed the same lineage patterns spanning from their base, that is juvenile domain, to their tip, that is adult domain, (Figure 4C–F) (N > 200 recombined filaments) indicating that growth stem cells maintain both their activity and their potency during a lifetime.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the lineage analysis in the Results section.

claim: Labelled cells in pattern 1 are epithelial cells covering the lamellae and the interlamellar space, including MRC cells.
source: Broadly speaking, labelled cells in pattern 1 (Figure 4C,G–H) are epithelial cells covering the lamellae and the interlamellar space, including MRC cells as revealed by expression of the Na+/K + ATPase (Figure 4H).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4C,G-H.

claim: Pattern 2 consists of labelled pillar cells and chondrocytes of the gill ray.
source: Pattern 2 consists of labelled pillar cells and chondrocytes of the gill ray (Figure 4I,I', and reconstructions in Video 3), both easily distinguishable by their location and unique nuclear morphology.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4I,I'.

claim: Pillar cells and chondrocytes were previously reported as neural crest derivatives.
source: Both cell types were previously reported as neural crest derivatives (Mongera et al., 2013)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by a citation.

claim: Pillar cells and chondrocytes are produced by a common stem cell in every filament during the post-embryonic growth of medaka.
source: and our results demonstrate that they are produced by a common stem cell in every filament during the post-embryonic growth of medaka.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the lineage analysis in the Results section.

claim: 97.4% of branchial arch extremes that started with a labelled filament were followed by a filament with the same recombination pattern.
source: We have focussed on 153 branchial arch extremes that started with a labelled filament (N = 83 for rec. pattern 1, N = 44 for rec. pattern 2, N = 22 for rec. pattern three and N = 4 for rec. pattern 4), and 97.4% were followed by a filament with the same recombination pattern (Figure 5B–E) (Supplementary file 6).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5B-E.

claim: 81.7% of stretches maintained the same recombination pattern for six or more filaments.
source: Moreover, 81.7% of stretches maintained the same recombination pattern for six or more filaments, indicating that the labelled cell-of-origin for post-embryonic filaments was already fate-restricted.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: The labelled cell-of-origin for post-embryonic filaments was already fate-restricted.
source: Moreover, 81.7% of stretches maintained the same recombination pattern for six or more filaments, indicating that the labelled cell-of-origin for post-embryonic filaments was already fate-restricted.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the data in the Results section.

claim: A branchial arch contains fate-restricted growth br-archSCs at its peripheral extremes that produce growth filamSCs stem cells with the same fate-restriction.
source: Altogether, our data revealed that a branchial arch contains fate-restricted growth br-archSCs at its peripheral extremes that produce growth filamSCs stem cells with the same fate-restriction.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the lineage analysis in the Results section.

claim: Fate-restriction had already occurred when brachial arches were formed.
source: We have observed cases in which the same recombination pattern is displayed along the entire branchial arch (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B)(pattern 1 N = 1 branchial arch, pattern 3 N = 2 branchial arches, pattern 4 N = 1 branchial arch), indicating that fate-restriction had already occurred when brachial arches were formed.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the lineage analysis in the Results section.

claim: Lineage analysis involving blastula transplantation, heat-shock-induced recombination during early embryonic stages and tamoxifen-induced recombination during late embryonic stages indicated the existence of fate-restricted gill stem cells that have independent embryonic origins.
source: Therefore, our lineage analysis involving blastula transplantation, heat-shock-induced recombination during early embryonic stages and tamoxifen-induced recombination during late embryonic stages indicated the existence of fate-restricted gill stem cells that have independent embryonic origins.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from multiple lineage analysis approaches in the Results section.

claim: P53 is not critical to maintain fate-restriction in gill stem cells.
source: In both cases, we obtained branchial arches displaying filaments labelled in one pattern only (Figure 6A,B), which indicates that P53 is not critical to maintain fate-restriction in gill stem cells.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the chimera experiments in the Results section.

claim: In p53-/-- to-WT chimeras, composite filaments with an EGFP+ labelled mutant lineage and three non-labelled lineages were indistinguishable from neighbour wild-type filaments in both length and morphology.
source: We focussed on filaments labelled in pattern 2 (Figure 6A) (N = 4 filaments in two branchial arches) and observed that in both length and morphology chimeras were indistinguishable from neighbour wild-type filaments in the same branchial arch.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 6A.

claim: In WT-to-p53-/- chimeras, composite filaments were clearly shorter than their wild type neighbours.
source: Notably, however, in branchial arches of WT-to-p53-/- chimeras, composite filaments were clearly shorter than their wild type neighbours (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Shorter filaments in WT-to-p53-/- chimeras were filaments in which pattern 2 came from donor cells and the rest of the lineages were from the host.
source: Shorter filaments were filaments in which pattern 2 came from donor cells and the rest of the lineages were from the host (Figure 6B'–B''') (19/19 filaments labelled in pattern 2 were shorter than their immediate neighbours).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 6B'-B'''.

claim: Composite filaments in which pattern 3 came from donor cells displayed a regular size.
source: Composite filaments in which pattern 3 came from donor cells displayed a regular size (Figure 6B'–B''') (58/58 filaments labelled in pattern 3 were indistinguishable from their neighbours).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 6B'-B'''.

claim: Manipulating just one lineage in the organ results in a massive growth phenotype.
source: Thus, our data from WT-to-p53-/- chimeras reveal that manipulating just one lineage in the organ results in a massive growth phenotype.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the chimera experiments in the Results section.

claim: The different lineages may have unequal roles during filament growth.
source: Critically, as these growth defects are limited to the filaments labelled in pattern 2 these data suggest that the different lineages may have unequal roles during filament growth.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the chimera experiments in the Results section.

claim: The length of consecutive lamellae does not increase with time along a filament.
source: Noticeable, the length of consecutive lamellae does not increase with time along a filament (Figure 7B), resulting in basal and apical lamellae having comparable sizes (basal: 35,72 ± 1,93 um and apical: 34,38 ± 4,04 um N = 6 lamellae of each).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Basal and apical lamellae have comparable sizes.
source: Noticeable, the length of consecutive lamellae does not increase with time along a filament (Figure 7B), resulting in basal and apical lamellae having comparable sizes (basal: 35,72 ± 1,93 um and apical: 34,38 ± 4,04 um N = 6 lamellae of each).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with quantitative data.

claim: Most lamellae contained positive cells at the proximal extreme after 12 hr IdU pulse.
source: To address the presence and location of proliferating cells in the lamellae of medaka, we performed shorter IdU pulses (12 hr) and observed that most lamellae contained positive cells at the proximal extreme (Figure 7C), adjacent to the central blood vessels and the gill ray.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Homeostatic pillar stem cells are present at the base of each lamella in medaka gills.
source: Our results, therefore, indicate the presence of homeostatic pillar stem cells at the base of each lamella in medaka gills.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the lineage analysis in the Results section.

claim: Growth stem cells are displaced by the progeny they generate.
source: We then wondered about their different behaviour; while growth stem cells are displaced by the progeny they generate, homeostatic stem cells maintain their position while pushing their progeny away.
evidence: This is stated as an observation in the Results section.

claim: Homeostatic stem cells maintain their position while pushing their progeny away.
source: We then wondered about their different behaviour; while growth stem cells are displaced by the progeny they generate, homeostatic stem cells maintain their position while pushing their progeny away.
evidence: This is stated as an observation in the Results section.

claim: The growing edge where growth stem cells host is subjected to less spatial restriction than the gill ray niche.
source: It has indeed been shown in other teleost fish that the growing edge where growth stem cells host is subjected to less spatial restriction than the gill ray niche (Morgan, 1974).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by a citation.

claim: There is a strong extracellular matrix rich in collagen secreted mainly by chondrocytes and early pillar cells across the filament.
source: On the other hand, there is a strong extracellular matrix rich in collagen and secreted mainly by chondrocytes and early pillar cells across the filament (Morgan, 1974), adjacent to the place in which we characterised homeostatic stem cells.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by a citation.

claim: Ablated filaments restored the characteristic morphology of a growth domain at their most upper extreme after one month.
source: When experimental fish were grown for a month after ablation, we could still recognise the ablated filaments due to their shorter length, compared to that of their neighbour, non-ablated filaments (Figure 8B). Ablated filaments, however, restored the characteristic morphology of a growth domain at their most upper extreme (Figure 8C,D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 8C,D.

claim: The new growth domains after ablation were proliferative, showing a similar IdU label than non-ablated filaments in the same branchial arch.
source: Additionally, IdU incorporation showed that the new growth domains were proliferative, showing a similar IdU label than non-ablated filaments in the same branchial arch (Figure 8E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 8E.

claim: The recombination pattern of the basal, non-injured region was identical to the recombination pattern of the newly generated zone after ablation.
source: When we analysed these samples 3 weeks after injury, we observed that the recombination pattern of the basal, non-injured region was identical to the recombination pattern of the newly generated zone (Figure 8F–I) (N = 30 filaments in six branchial arches, N = 17 for pattern 1, N = 11 for pattern 2, N = 2 for pattern 3).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 8F-I.

claim: The re-established growth zone is formed by an ensemble of cells from the different lineages.
source: These results indicate that the re-established growth zone is formed by an ensemble of cells from the different lineages, and strongly suggest that homeostatic stem cells within all lineages can be converted to growth stem cells during regeneration.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the ablation experiments in the Results section.

claim: Homeostatic stem cells within all lineages can be converted to growth stem cells during regeneration.
source: These results indicate that the re-established growth zone is formed by an ensemble of cells from the different lineages, and strongly suggest that homeostatic stem cells within all lineages can be converted to growth stem cells during regeneration.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the ablation experiments in the Results section.

claim: Filaments possess the ability to resume growth from the homeostatic domain in a process that requires cells from different lineages.
source: Our data definitively reveal that filaments possess the ability to resume growth from the homeostatic domain in a process that requires cells from different lineages.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the ablation experiments in the Results section.

claim: The different niches along the filament could operate as main regulators of the homeostatic-or-growth activity for stem cells in the fish gill.
source: Overall, we propose from our observations that the different niches – physical and/or molecular - along the filament could operate as main regulators of the homeostatic-or-growth activity for stem cells in the fish gill.
evidence: This is stated as a proposal based on the experimental observations in the Results section.

claim: The peripheral-to-central axis of branchial arches reflects a young-to-old filament order.
source: The peripheral-to-central axis of branchial arches reflects a young-to-old filament order, and the longitudinal axis of a filament reflects a young-to-old lamellae order.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a summary of the findings.

claim: The longitudinal axis of a filament reflects a young-to-old lamellae order.
source: The peripheral-to-central axis of branchial arches reflects a young-to-old filament order, and the longitudinal axis of a filament reflects a young-to-old lamellae order.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a summary of the findings.

claim: The two growth stem cells and the one homeostatic stem cell types are clonal and organised in a hierarchical manner.
source: The two growth stem cells and the one homeostatic stem cell types are clonal and organised in a hierarchical manner.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a summary of the findings.

claim: The relative position within the organ has a major impact on the growth vs homeostatic activity of stem cells.
source: Our observations indicate that the relative position within the organ has a major impact on the growth vs homeostatic activity of stem cells.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an interpretation of the findings.

claim: When the growth domain of a filament is lost, the homeostatic domain is able to generate a new, functional growth domain.
source: We have found that when the growth domain of a filament is lost, the homeostatic domain is able to generate a new, functional growth domain.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a summary of the ablation experiments.

claim: Physical or molecular modifications in the local environment could convert homeostatic stem cells into growth stem cells.
source: This observation suggests that physical or molecular modifications in the local environment (relaxation of the inner core, or the absence of a repressive signal, respectively) could convert homeostatic stem cells into growth stem cells.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an interpretation of the ablation experiments.

claim: Restricting growth stem cells to the growing edge is an effective way to compartmentalise cell addition and organ function.
source: Restricting growth stem cells to the growing edge is an effective way to compartmentalise cell addition and organ function.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an interpretation of the findings.

claim: The location of growth stem cells in gill filaments is highly reminiscent of the overall topology of meristems in plants.
source: Strikingly, the location of growth stem cells in gill filaments is highly reminiscent of the overall topology of meristems in plants (Greb and Lohmann, 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a comparison to plant systems, supported by a citation.

claim: In both gill filaments and plant meristems, axis extension occurs by the sustained activity of stem cells that locate to the growing edge.
source: In both systems, axis extension occurs by the sustained activity of stem cells that locate to the growing edge.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a comparison between the two systems.

claim: Stem cells in both gill filaments and plant meristems consistently remain at the growing zone, while their progeny start differentiation programs and occupy a final location at the coordinates in which they were born.
source: These stem cells consistently remain at the growing zone, while their progeny start differentiation programs and occupy a final location at the coordinates in which they were born.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a comparison between the two systems.

claim: Other ever-growing organs in fish follow the same growing principle, with tissue stem cells located at the growing edge and differentiated progeny left behind.
source: It is to note that other ever-growing organs in fish follow the same growing principle, with tissue stem cells located at the growing edge and differentiated progeny left behind, as it has been nicely shown for different cell types in the zebrafish caudal fin (Tu and Johnson, 2011) and the medaka neural retina and retinal epithelium (Centanin et al., 2011; Centanin et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by citations.

claim: Stem cells are thought to have evolved independently in the vegetal and the animal lineages.
source: Since stem cells are thought to have evolved independently in the vegetal and the animal lineages (Meyerowitz, 2002; Scheres, 2007), our results illustrate how the same rationale to sustain permanent growth can be adopted in the most diverse systems.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by citations.

claim: The same rationale to sustain permanent growth can be adopted in the most diverse systems.
source: Since stem cells are thought to have evolved independently in the vegetal and the animal lineages (Meyerowitz, 2002; Scheres, 2007), our results illustrate how the same rationale to sustain permanent growth can be adopted in the most diverse systems.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an interpretation of the findings.

claim: At least four different fate-restricted gill stem cells were identified, which generate reproducible labelling patterns along gill filaments.
source: We used diverse un-biased labelling approaches (sub-optimal tamoxifen concentrations using an ubiquitously-expressed inducible ErT2CRE, heat-shock-induced expression of CRE, transplantation of few permanently-labelled cells at the blastula stage) to identify at least four different fate-restricted gill stem cells, which generate reproducible labelling patterns along gill filaments.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a summary of the findings.

claim: The four fate-restricted gill stem cells do not share a common early progenitor, but rather have independent embryonic origins.
source: Our experiments indicate that these stem cells do not share a common early progenitor, but rather have independent embryonic origins.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a conclusion from the lineage analysis.

claim: The growth zone of a gill filament is an ensemble — a group of stem cells with different potencies that work in an interconnected manner.
source: Since each filament contains all four fate-restricted stem cells (we have not observed filaments lacking one entire lineage), our results determine that the growth zone of a gill filament is indeed an ensemble — a group of stem cells with different potencies that work in an interconnected manner.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a conclusion from the findings.

claim: The prediction for gill filaments is that they contained a very reduced number of stem cells, for they generate all-or-none labelled filaments of a given cell type reflecting a clonal nature.
source: The prediction for gill filaments is that they contained a very reduced number of stem cells, for they generate all-or-none labelled filaments of a given cell type reflecting a clonal nature.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an inference from the experimental observations.

claim: P53 is necessary to establish/maintain the coordinated growth of neighbour filaments.
source: Our experiments revealed that P53 is indeed necessary to establish/maintain the coordinated growth of neighbour filaments.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a conclusion from the chimera experiments.

claim: Growth phenotypes were observed only when the lineage of pillar cells was involved in p53 chimeras.
source: Strikingly, we observed growth phenotypes only when the lineage of pillar cells was involved: p53 mutant filaments that contain wild-type pillar cells can not growth at the same pace than fully p53 mutant filaments in the same branchial arch.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a summary of the chimera experiments.

claim: Wild-type cells in other lineages did not produce the same phenotype as wild-type pillar cells in p53 chimeras.
source: Wild-type cells in other lineages did not produce the same phenotype, which we interpret as a differential hierarchical organisation of the different fate-restricted stem cells sustaining filament growth.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a summary of the chimera experiments.

claim: There is a differential hierarchical organisation of the different fate-restricted stem cells sustaining filament growth.
source: Wild-type cells in other lineages did not produce the same phenotype, which we interpret as a differential hierarchical organisation of the different fate-restricted stem cells sustaining filament growth.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an interpretation of the chimera experiments.

claim: Filament growth is autonomous - that is a filament's growth rate does not adjust to the size of its neighbour filaments.
source: Additionally, our experiments working with genetic chimeras and also the ones in which we ablate the growth domain of wild type filaments show that filament growth is a autonomous - that is a filament's growth rate does not adjust to the size of its neighbour filaments.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a conclusion from the experiments.

claim: Growth and homeostatic stem cells are clonal along a filament, where the former generate the latter.
source: Our lineage analysis demonstrates that growth and homeostatic stem cells are clonal along a filament, where the former generate the latter.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a summary of the findings.

claim: Growth stem cells are located at the growing tip, beyond the rigid core that physically sustains the structure of the filament.
source: The most obvious difference between these two stem cell types is their relative position; growth stem cells are located at the growing tip, beyond the rigid core that physically sustains the structure of the filament, while homeostatic stem cells are embedded inside the tissue, adjacent to the collagen-rich chondrocyte column.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a summary of the findings.

claim: Homeostatic stem cells are embedded inside the tissue, adjacent to the collagen-rich chondrocyte column.
source: The most obvious difference between these two stem cell types is their relative position; growth stem cells are located at the growing tip, beyond the rigid core that physically sustains the structure of the filament, while homeostatic stem cells are embedded inside the tissue, adjacent to the collagen-rich chondrocyte column.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a summary of the findings.

claim: Both the function and the relative location of the gill homeostatic stem cells match those of the mammalian homeostatic stem cells.
source: It is to note that both the function and the relative location of the gill homeostatic stem cells match those of the mammalian homeostatic stem cells, being located at a fixed position and displacing their progeny far away - as it is observed for intestinal stem cells, skin stem cells and oesophagus stem cells among others (Barker et al., 2008; Blanpain and Fuchs, 2009; Seery, 2002).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by citations.

claim: The functional comparison of growth and homeostatic stem cells in the gill suggests the existence of a physical niche that would restrict stem cells to their homeostatic role, preventing them to drive growth.
source: The functional comparison of growth and homeostatic stem cells in the gill suggests the existence of a physical niche that would restrict stem cells to their homeostatic role, preventing them to drive growth.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an interpretation of the findings.

claim: RNA-seq data comparing the transcriptomes from the growth domain and the central domains revealed numerous Integrins and membrane proteins overrepresented at the growing edge.
source: Indeed, our RNA-seq data comparing the transcriptomes from the growth domain and the central domains revealed numerous Integrins and membrane proteins overrepresented at the growing edge, supporting the notion of a different physical niche mediating filament growth.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion based on RNA-seq data.

claim: During vertebrate evolution, the transition from lower (ever-growing) to higher (size-fixed) vertebrates involved restraining the growth activity of adult stem cells.
source: We believe that during vertebrate evolution, the transition from lower (ever-growing) to higher (size-fixed) vertebrates involved restraining the growth activity of adult stem cells.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a hypothesis.

claim: One of the main functions of mammalian physical niches would be to restrict stem cells to their homeostatic function.
source: One of the main functions of mammalian physical niches, in this view, would be to restrict stem cells to their homeostatic function.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a hypothesis.

claim: Many stem-cell-related pathological conditions in mammals involve changes in the microenvironment including physical aspects of the niche.
source: Many stem-cell-related pathological conditions in mammals involve changes in the microenvironment including physical aspects of the niche (Brabletz et al., 2001; Vermeulen et al., 2010; Ye et al., 2015; Oskarsson et al., 2011; Liu et al., 2012; Butcher et al., 2009)
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by citations.

claim: Homeostatic stem cells could drive growth in pathological conditions.
source: Many stem-cell-related pathological conditions in mammals involve changes in the microenvironment including physical aspects of the niche (Brabletz et al., 2001; Vermeulen et al., 2010; Ye et al., 2015; Oskarsson et al., 2011; Liu et al., 2012; Butcher et al., 2009), suggesting that homeostatic stem cells could drive growth in that context.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an inference from cited literature.

claim: Healthy aSCs have the capacity to drive growth under experimental conditions and when removed from their physiological niche.
source: Along the same line, the extensive work using organoids that are generated from adult homeostatic stem cells, like intestinal stem cells, (Sato et al., 2009; Kretzschmar and Clevers, 2016), demonstrates that healthy aSCs have indeed the capacity to drive growth under experimental conditions and when removed from their physiological niche.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by citations.

claim: Different niches affect the functional output of clonal stem cells driving growth and homeostatic replacement in an intact in vivo model.
source: Our work, therefore, illustrates how different niches affect the functional output of clonal stem cells driving growth and homeostatic replacement in an intact in vivo model.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a summary of the study's contribution.

claim: Adult p53E241X medaka display branchial arches that have the same morphology and a comparable size than wild-type branchial arches.
source: The p53E241X medaka mutant is viable and fertile (Taniguchi et al., 2006), and adult p53E241X display branchial arches that have the same morphology and a comparable size than wild-type branchial arches in medaka (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.
